name: Question 8
problem:
Use the Laplace transform of $f(t)={e}^{\text{i}\omega t}$ to find the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t).$$\,L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)}=$ {{field-1}},
defined for {{field-2}}.
worked_solution:
The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions $f(t)$ and $g(t),$ we have

$$
L{\alpha f(t)+\beta g(t)}=\alpha \cdot L{f(t)}+\beta \cdot L{g(t)},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)=\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}-{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}
$$

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)} & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}-{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}-\frac{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =L{\frac{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}}-L{\frac{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}{2\text{i}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall that 

$$
L{{e}^{\text{i}\omega t}}=\frac{1}{s-\text{i}\omega },\,s>0.
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s-12\text{i}},\,s>0 \\ L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}} & =\frac{1}{s+12\text{i}},\,s>0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡(12t)} & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{12\text{i}t}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}L{{e}^{-12\text{i}t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s-12\text{i}}-\frac{1}{2\text{i}}\cdot \frac{1}{s+12\text{i}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{1}{s-12\text{i}}-\frac{1}{s+12\text{i}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{(s+12\text{i})-(s-12\text{i})}{(s-12\text{i})(s+12\text{i})}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\text{i}}(\frac{24\text{i}}{{s}^{2}+144}) \\  & =\frac{12}{{s}^{2}+144},\end{aligned}
$$

defined for $s>0.$

EXPLANATION

The linearity property of the Laplace transform states that for functions f(t) and g(t), we have L{αf(t)+βg(t)}=α⋅L{f(t)}+β⋅L{g(t)}, where α and β are constants.

First, recall that the sine function can be defined in terms of complex exponentials as follows: sin⁡(12t)=e12it−e−12it2i

Taking the Laplace transform and applying the linearity property, we have L{sin⁡(12t)}=L{e12it−e−12it2i}=L{e12it2i−e−12it2i}=L{e12it2i}−L{e−12it2i}=12iL{e12it}−12iL{e−12it}.

Now, we recall that L{eiωt}=1s−iω,s>0. Therefore, we have the following: L{e12it}=1s−12i,s>0L{e−12it}=1s+12i,s>0

Therefore, the Laplace transform of sin⁡(12t) is L{sin⁡(12t)}=12iL{e12it}−12iL{e−12it}=12i⋅1s−12i−12i⋅1s+12i=12i(1s−12i−1s+12i)=12i((s+12i)−(s−12i)(s−12i)(s+12i))=12i(24is2+144)=12s2+144, defined for s>0.
